title: Historical Context: Sylvester's 1884 Coin Problem
content: The Frobenius coin problem (also called the Money Changing Problem or Postage Stamp Problem) asks: given denominations with gcd = 1, what is the largest amount that cannot be made? Sylvester's 1884 solution for two coprime denominations a and b is the clean formula g(a,b) = ab - a - b. Despite the elementary statement, the three-generator case (n ≥ 3) has no known closed-form solution and computing g(a,b,c) is NP-hard in general.
mathContext: For $\gcd(a,b) = 1$: $g(a,b) = ab - a - b$. Equivalent form: $g(a,b) = (a-1)(b-1) - 1$. Count of non-representable positives: $(a-1)(b-1)/2$.

title: Representable: The Coin Combination Predicate
content: Representable a b n is the existential `∃ x y : ℕ, n = a*x + b*y` — can you make n using only a-cent and b-cent coins with non-negative amounts? The closure theorems show: 0, a, b are always representable; representable numbers are closed under adding a or b. These five lemmas are the base cases for the inductive argument showing all sufficiently large numbers are representable.

title: Injectivity → Surjectivity: The Bijection Engine
content: The private lemma `mul_mod_injective` proves that k ↦ k*b mod a is injective on Fin a when gcd(a,b) = 1. Proof: if k₁*b ≡ k₂*b (mod a), then a | b*(k₁-k₂), and since gcd(a,b) = 1, `Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_right` gives a | (k₁-k₂). Since |k₁-k₂| < a, this forces k₁ = k₂. Then `Finite.injective_iff_surjective` converts injectivity to surjectivity on the finite set Fin a, giving `exists_mul_mod`: every residue r < a is achieved as k*b mod a.
mathContext: $\gcd(a,b) = 1 \Rightarrow (k_1 b \equiv k_2 b \pmod{a} \Rightarrow k_1 \equiv k_2 \pmod{a}) \Rightarrow$ bijection on $\{0,\ldots,a-1\}$.

title: Large Representable: The Residue Class Argument
content: For n ≥ (a-1)(b-1), find k < a with k*b ≡ n (mod a) (from surjectivity). Then a | (n - k*b). The crucial step: why is n ≥ k*b? By contradiction — if k*b > n, then a | (k*b - n), so a ≤ k*b - n. But k ≤ a-1 gives k*b ≤ (a-1)b = (a-1)(b-1) + (a-1) ≤ n + (a-1) < n + a, so k*b < n + a and k*b - n < a. Contradiction with a ≤ k*b - n. Thus n = aq + k*b for some q ≥ 0.
mathContext: Given $n \geq (a-1)(b-1)$: find $k < a$ with $kb \equiv n \pmod{a}$. Claim $kb \leq n$: else $a \leq kb - n \leq (a-1)b - n \leq (a-1)(b-1) + (a-1) - n < a$. Contradiction. So $n = aq + kb$ with $q \geq 0$.

title: Non-Representability: Coprimality Forces Contradiction
content: Suppose ab - a - b = ax + by. Then a*b = a*(x+1) + b*(y+1). Since a | a*b and a | a*(x+1), we get a | b*(y+1). By coprimality (gcd(a,b)=1), `Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left` gives a | (y+1), so y+1 ≥ a. Similarly b | (x+1), so x+1 ≥ b. Then a*(x+1) + b*(y+1) ≥ a*b + b*a = 2ab > ab. But it equals ab. Contradiction by `linarith`.
mathContext: If $ax + by = ab - a - b$, then $a(x+1) + b(y+1) = ab$. But $a \mid (y+1)$ and $b \mid (x+1)$ force $a(x+1) \geq ab$ and $b(y+1) \geq ab$, so their sum $\geq 2ab > ab$.

title: Sylvester's Theorem: The Complete Statement
content: `sylvester_frobenius` combines the two halves into a conjunction: frobeniusNumber a b equals ab-a-b AND is not representable AND every n > frobeniusNumber a b is representable. The proof bundles `frobenius_not_representable` and `large_representable` (after converting the bound `n > ab-a-b` to `(a-1)*(b-1) ≤ n` via omega). The `rfl` proof of equality is because frobeniusNumber is defined as a*b - a - b.
mathContext: $g(a,b) = ab - a - b$, $\neg\text{Rep}(a,b,g)$, $n > g \Rightarrow \text{Rep}(a,b,n)$ — all in one triple conjunction.

title: Verified Examples via native_decide
content: Concrete computations validate the formula: g(3,5) = 7 (7 is the largest amount not makeable with 3- and 5-cent coins), g(3,7) = 11, g(5,8) = 27. The numNonRepresentable examples confirm (a-1)(b-1)/2: for (3,5) this is (2)(4)/2 = 4 non-representable positives {1,2,4,7}; for (3,7) it's 6. The `native_decide` tactic compiles these to native code for fast verified computation.
